utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, may I remind the Defence that the issue of what pages of P482, which is a book, the Defence would wish to tender in addition to what was tendered by the Prosecution still remains unresolved and that a recent reminder has not triggered any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, after the reminder that was sent by Mr. Nilsson, I sent an e-mail to the persons in OTP who were also copied on Mr. Nilsson's e-mail with a proposal, and I have not heard yet from OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can resolve this matter soon. Then I take it that -- yes. Mr. Theunens, good morning to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony still binds you. Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I may have exhibit P878 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm showing you or about to show you a document authored by General Lausic on the 16th of August, and was sent to all military police units and to all military police administration departments and sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we scroll down to the bottom of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In it, Mr. Lausic notes that: "With the change in the deployment of Croatian army units in the newly liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia, and the organisation of police administrations, police stations, and MUP -- of the MUP of the RH, conditions have been created for a change in the deployment of units of the military police of the armed forces ... as well as the manner in carrying out military police tasks and in keeping with that I here order ..." Then he goes through and to the various military police battalion, he gives assignments. Point 4 says, for example, "By 1800 hours on the 18th of August, abolish all check-points towards free areas of the BH Federation in the zones of responsibility of the 67th, 70th, and 71st Military Police Battalions. The check-points shall be taken over by staff of the RH MUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go over to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Point 6, and this is -- I'd ask to you keep this point in mind because it is relevant to the next document. It says: "In all zones of responsibility, ensure that commanders of military police units are familiar with the deployment of HV units on the line of defence and at camp sites, the strength of the units, the time and direction of redeployment or departure of VP units from the zone of responsibility, and that they have the telephone numbers of the commander and vice versa, thus ensuring knowledge of the zone of responsibility on the basis of which the engagement of VP patrols shall also be planned." And before I pose a question to you, let me now take you to Exhibit P877.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm know showing you a document from two days after this document. And if you recall the sequence, the one on the screen right now was the 16th of August. Mr. Moric sends a letter to General Lausic, I believe, on the 17th of August. Now I'm showing you the 18th of August, where General Lausic issues orders where he references that letter from Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we scroll to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see this is also now sent also to -- it's an order sent to all -- the military police battalions there: 67, 68, 69, 71, and 72. He references in the introduction: "The military police administration received an official document from the MUP of RH on 17 August 1995, stating that in the territory of the Republic of Croatia liberated during Operation Oluja, still there are daily recorded examples of houses being burned, of illegal taking away of the other people's movable property, as well as other -- as well as examples of other forms of illegal behaviour committed by the members of the HVO and by the civilians wearing the HV uniforms ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I seem to have a different translation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll read the one on the screen then?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The English text says "HV."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I seem to have an earlier translation, so I will read the one that says -- it's not relevant to the question I'm going to pose, but you're right. The one on the screen says: "... other unlawful actions by HV soldiers and civilians wearing HV uniforms are occurring on a daily basis." The communication also says that "cooperation between the military and civilian police on liberated territory thus far has not yielded results, pursuant to the fundamental guidelines of state policy." It goes on and he issues an order to the military police battalions that I referenced. And if you look through the order, he gives specific tasks including that "the commanders of the military platoons companies and battalions are immediately required to get in touch with commanders ever police stations." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he also states, and I also copied that in my report in English page 230, in the second part that "commanders of platoons, companies, and battalions of the military police are to immediately get in contact with the highest ranking HV commander in their area of responsibility," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I wasn't finished with my question. I thought you were disagreeing with what I had read up to that point?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now you're right. The next sentence says -- but you didn't finish the sentence there. It says: "... get in contact with the highest ranking HV commander in their area of responsibility, and completely execute item 6 of the UVP order," which is item 6 of the order I just showed you on the screen, which said: "Get in contact with the commanders so you know ..." -- essentially it says, so you know where the troops will be, so you can plan your activities accordingly. Correct? It doesn't say, Go to the local area commander so can you receive orders from him on what you're supposed to be doing. And if I may complete this, further to the point, if you look at 3, it says -- he gives specific instructions: "Minutes are to be composed indicating in detail the conclusions of the meetings held with the chiefs of police stations and heads of police administrations," according to item 1, "as well as minutes of the meetings held with commanders of HV," according to item 2 of the order. Then it says: "Minutes from the meetings are to be collected to the commands of the battalion, (independent companies); and once compiled, they should be submitted to the military police administration by 2000 hours on 19 August 1995." Now, isn't what this is saying that General Lausic is issuing orders to the battalions that they're to coordinate with MUP police stations and police administrations; they are to get in contact with the local HV commanders, pursuant to the 16 August, order to get information as to the -- where the troops HV troops are deployed; and then they are to report back not to the local commanders, they're to report back to General Lausic about the implementation of this order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a problem in a sense that we're taking this document, but it is obvious that General Lausic cannot reiterate everything that is put, for example, in the rules in the 1994 rules on the use of the military police, because then he would have to issue encyclopedias. I think I can better answer the question by directing you to 65 ter 2741, which is described on page 328 in the second part of my report, where the commander of the 3rd Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion reports to Major Juric about his cooperation and coordination with both the operational commander, i.e., the commander of OG Zadar, Major Fuzul, as well as with the chief of the civilian police. That report gives a very good picture as to how the regulations as well as the following orders are being implemented already at the earlier stages of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I have to cut you off again because you're going off on a 65 ter that has nothing do with the question I have posed to you. That is, as you know, a report from a subordinate military police commander to Major Juric, and I was going to ask you this morning. You've already testified that Major Juric never reported to General Gotovina. So why you keep going back to that document is beyond me. Let's go back now. That is the 8th of August. I'm asking about the 16th to 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Your Honours, I'm trying to explain based on the documents I reviewed, and also on my -- my professional and educational background how things are being implemented. If we want to be 100 percent precise, Mr. Misetic, with this particular order we have on the screen, and then with P878, I would like to see P878 again and see to what extent it includes instructions for the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and whether it is, indeed, sent to the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Because on the image I saw on the monitor, I could only see duties and tasks for the 69th, the 70th, and the 71th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, whether you could see it or not, before I take you back to that document, look at the class and order number referenced in number 2, dated 16 August, and then I want you to compare it back to P878. Then tell me if you deny that P877 was sent to the 72nd Military Police Battalion with the instruction to follow number 6, item 6 in the 16 August, and tell me if that is the same document that he's referenced on the 18th August that I showed on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if the witness is convinced that although the same numbers appear, that nevertheless there is a question to be raised as to whether the one document is addressed to a unit which apparently knows about document and refers to it, then he is entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. That's fine. I want him, so we're not flipping back and forth in documents, to keep in mind the number in number 2. Now, Mr. Registrar, if we can go to P878, to the first page, which I've already read to Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You see, in the top, it says: "To all military police units."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. But the specific instructions on the first page only apply to the addressees we can see or the units we can see: The 69th, the 67th, the 71st, and I can't see if there's a number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. In those specific paragraphs, for specific tasks, to those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we can go to page 3, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph starts off: "In all zone of responsibilities."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it was sent to all military police battalions; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you about the title. It says "to all military police battalion." However, when we see the list of addressees at the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's no military unit in any addressee at the end, so we should say that it didn't go to any military police unit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no reference to the Split Military District. I don't claim that that has an important impact as to whether paragraph 6 applied to the 72nd Military Police Battalion or not. I don't -- in my view, based on the other documents I have reviewed, paragraph 6 does not change anything to the regular military police tasks the military police battalion were to execute in the zones of responsible of the military districts, including the Split Military District; again, these duties, as they are determined in the 1994 rules on the military police. And as I mentioned, 65 ter 2741 is an example showing how these tasks, the tasks you mentioned on Wednesday, the establishment of check-points, how that is coordinated with the operational commander and with the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to the document that -- and I question that I asked you. In this document from the 18th of August, after Mr. Lausic receives a report from Mr. Moric, it's him issuing instructions to -- I'm sorry, issuing orders to the military police battalions on how they're to coordinate with the MUP, how they're to report on their meetings, and that they are to meet with the highest ranking local commanders to gain information about where HV troops are located. Isn't that what this document says?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what the document says and that is in line with the professional -- I mean, the professional chain. As you mention yourself, the how, that is what is being instructed through the professional chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I mentioned, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar if we could go to Exhibit D595, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are -- this is a report of the results of a coordination meeting between the representatives of the MUP and the ministry -- sorry, and the military police administration, regarding continued problems in the newly liberated areas. That meeting took place on the 15th of September, 1995. On the first page, you see who attended this meeting. Mr. Moric was present; his assistant for crime police, Mr. Benko, was present. On behalf of the military administration, it was General Lausic, his assistant Mr. Biskic -- sorry. On behalf of the MUPs, chiefs of police administrations were present in the areas -- from the newly liberated areas; their deputies and assistants commanders from the military police chief of departments of the MP administration; commanders of 69th, 70th, 71st, and 72nd MP Battalions; and chiefs of the military police crime investigation departments. It records who said what at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn to page 5 of seven, I would like to show you what General Lausic said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "General Lausic concluded the reports of the MP units' commanders. Members of the MUP and the military police are the promoters of the state policy, and the only people responsible for its implementation are present at this meeting. The objective is clear: Protection of people and property and creation of positive security situation in the entire area of the Republic of Croatia." What do you think General Lausic means when he says that the only people responsible for the implementation of that state policy are present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have referred to this document in my report on page 238 of the second part, English page. It is what Mr. Lausic states. When I compare his statement with the regulations and all the other documents have I seen, and in particular orders by the chief of the Main Staff and the commander of the Split Military District, as well as subordinate commanders in relation to the enforcement of discipline, I cannot draw any particular conclusions from it, except that, in his view, he is -- he and the civilian police are, as he puts it, the promotors of the state policy and only people responsible. However, the military documents I have seen show that also the chief of the Main Staff, as well as the subordinate commanders, considered themselves responsible to prevent looting, to prevent burning, and to enforce all other aspects of military discipline as is stipulated in the Code of Discipline and the other Croatian military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what I'm interested in more is your methodology, how you worked, how you drew your conclusions. I've spent the better part of a day now talking to you about military police. We've walked through Mr. Lausic' orders before Storm; orders during Storm to see specific facilities, specific warehouses; orders after Storm to coordinate with MUP to send him reports. We've talked about Mr. Juric's role and that he only reported to General Lausic. I'm now saying, when you reviewed those documents and came upon this passage, which I don't believe you quoted this passage in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you saw this passage, where General Lausic says, "The only people responsible for the implementation of this policy," which is to protect people and property, are present at this meeting ..." --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- yes, there is no doubt that he states it and that it is in the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. I know there is no doubt that he states it. My question to you is: When you're trying to piece this all together to see who is running the military police in -- in securing the territory during and after Operation Storm, what does that piece of information tell you about who's in command and control of the military police in its function to provide security and restore order in the liberated territories during and after Operation Storm? Regardless of the fact that you may think that there is other evidence that contradicts this, what did this piece of information tell you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the methodology consists of reviewing not just one document, which may -- or which shows a particular point of view or opinion or -- but it's about reviewing several documents, putting them in context, and, as I explained, drawing conclusions from those. Lausic, on the 15th of September, makes this statement; however, I have seen many other documents, both military documents - I mean, from the Military District command and the subordinate commands - as well as from the military police, which show something else. Now, if I follow your logic, I should drop all these documents and only consider this one. Why? Because it focuses on the role of the military police. I think it is very important also to understand that in military environment, the military police, or SIS, or the department for political affairs, they do not operate as isolated, yeah, bodies, who do not communicate and who do not share information. The documents I have reviewed in the preparation of this report, as well as my background, show me that all these bodies cooperate on a continuous basis exchange information, and on a continuous basis interact with each other. That is what I have tried to show in my report; and, therefore, again, there is no doubt that General Lausic on the 15th of September makes this statement. However, based on the other material I have reviewed, I did not consider that this statement had a significant impact or had any impact on the conclusions I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now this is where I want to get more to your methodology. I want you to explain -- this isn't the only document, obviously. I spent all day Wednesday, all day -- or part of the day Tuesday showing you military police documents, Mr. Juric's role, the order sent by General Lausic, et cetera. So this is actually a document at the end in the context of the documents I showed you. But I want to get to a methodological question with you, and I want to compare two conclusions and explain to me how you arrive at those conclusions. When you see a document on direct examination that says, in the Grahovo area, guard the church, you concluded, well, that must mean they don't want negative public relations, so there was a policy to burn the houses, but protect the church, for PR reasons. On the basis of that entry, when I show you 25 documents capped by this sentence by General Lausic, you say to me, There could be other documents, and I don't want to draw the conclusion you're drawing. Why is 25 documents on one point and a direct quote from General Lausic not enough for you, but a line about protecting churches is enough to spin off a conclusion that it is a state policy to burn buildings but not churches?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure whether this is an accurate reflection of what I stated. I think it was the Presiding Judge who asked me about, or who challenged me at least, about the possible conclusion I drew in relation to the churches. I gave an example of one document. I couldn't identify it immediately, but any way, it is in my report. It is D810, which is mentioned on English page 394 in the second part the report; and D810 shows a general attitude in relation to the freedom of movement of the press. So I didn't testify that it was state policy to burn houses or to burn churches. I remember -- and these three's also quoted in my report, and, for example, in P7, in the operational diary. General Tolj instructs that churches should not be burned, and that brought about the whole discussion. In D810, it is stated that: In general, we have been directing reporters to places where Serbian barbarism was evident, torch Croatian villages," and so and so on. "We have also directed them to preserve Orthodox churches, Serbian civilians being given aid and food," and so on. I want to emphasise that the conclusion I drew on that conclusion on that entry in the diary of the Orthodox churches was a possible conclusion. The Presiding Judge challenged me, and I accepted the challenge. Here, we're talking about different documents. It is true that you have consistently shown me military police documents. I have tried to explain that when Juric, a military policeman, reports to Major-General Lausic about the activities of the military police, that these reports do not necessarily indicate who has orders -- who has ordered these activities. These reports also addressed the participation of military police units in combat tasks. I have only seen orders by operational commanders in relation to that aspect. You asked me on Wednesday whether I could find any orders by General Gotovina according to the so-called operational line. Well, I have reviewed my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if you want, I can read them out and address them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I didn't ask you that, and I anticipate and I know that you go back and then try to gather documents and interject them in to answers to questions that aren't related to the question I asked you. Okay. So let's's put a stop to that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was how you could reach general conclusions on the basis of one document; whereas, as Mr. Misetic put it is to you, where he showed you 25 documents which, in his view, apparently give a clear view on a certain matter why you would not accept what he considers to be the logical conclusion from these 25 documents. Mr. Misetic, the witness has been given an opportunity to answer the question. The point is clear. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have drawn our attention that, in your view, 25 convincing documents has not lead the witness; whereas, one document which you apparently consider not a proper basis for the conclusions that he has drawn, that's what you call methodology. That point is clear. I don't know how long --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's fine. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, this doesn't say anything about how to interpret question, answer, et cetera, but have you made clear what your view on the matter is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, let's change gears. Let's talk a little bit about the Code of Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit P1007, please, and if we could turn to Article 31, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, Article 31 is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll wait for it in Croatian as well. Page 5 of the Croatian version, in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Article 31 says: "In situations where the authorised officer finds that the offence against military discipline is also a criminal offence, the case shall be sent via regular channels to the authorised prosecutor. If he thinks that it is in the interest of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary procedures." Now what does that -- what is the relevance of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the relevance of that paragraph is that the authorised officer does not have to wait until there is a criminal procedure being started by the authorised prosecutor and the authorised officials; but that if he considers it necessary in order to maintain order and discipline in his unit, he can also immediately take the appropriate disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is not exactly what it says, is it, Mr. Theunens? It kind of says the opposite of what you're saying. It says: "If the disciplinary infraction is also a criminal offence, it shall be referred to the prosecutor." Then it says: "If he think," right? That's contrary to the rest of the disciplinary Code, would you agree with me, which imposes basically a requirement that other disciplinary infractions be sanctioned? Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't read it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, why would it have to say, "if he thinks it is in the interests of the service?" Why wouldn't it just say, "he shall issue a disciplinary sanction and refer the matter to the prosecution"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there are probably offences against military discipline which also represent the criminal offence or may represent a criminal offence, but which do not necessarily affect the interests of the service. I'm thinking, for example, if a military person has -- I've seen such a document where, I think, an officer was involved in domestic violence. Without going into details, it may well be that such an incident or such, yeah, a violation of discipline may represent a criminal offence, but does not affect the interests of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So domestic violence doesn't affect the interests of the service, but looting would affect the interest of the service?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're speaking in very general terms, but looting will certainly affect the interest of the service because, as I explained in my examination, looting happens during combat operations. When we use the term "looting," it means that it is a generalised activity, whereby the soldiers they see what they are doing. People see each other, and they keep an eye on how the commander reacts to this. Again, I'm talking from my own experience, not about looting, but other aspects of military discipline. If you, as a commander at the lowest possible level, do not enforce discipline, then the other soldiers who are not involved in violating discipline will see it as an encouragements to say, Well, if he can do it, I will do it, too. It is also important that, if at the lowest level, a commander tries to enforce discipline, that he is supported throughout the chain of command; otherwise, he will be lose his credibility. And in that context, in particular to the function of military discipline, I refer you to Article 7 of the Code of Discipline, which explains why it is important to enforce military discipline, not only against the perpetrators but also for the overall functioning of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, let me read to you the trial testimony of a former military prosecutor in Croatia, later a civilian prosecutor in Croatia, who told the Trial Chamber as follows: "Q. Can you say something about the following situation ..." This is the testimony of Zeljko Zganjer, beginning at page 11.576, line 6: "Q. Can you say something about the following situation: Let's say, for example, that a soldier or a military serviceman who were to be processed for a crime, and if a sentence was passed for that crime, would disciplinary proceedings be carried out before a military disciplinary court despite the fact that that person is already being tried for a crime? "A. I believe that proceedings before military courts for a crime, in a certain way enveloped any possible military disciplinary responsibility of a serviceman. In concrete terms, this would mean, if I'm not mistaken, if a person was found guilty and sentenced for a crime, then this would have enveloped that same person's responsibility for a possible disciplinary offence. In the category of crimes, a crime is the highest form of a punishable act, and, therefore, it is higher in the hierarchy than a disciplinary offence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to page 1157, beginning at line one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Q. Will that person be prosecuted for a disciplinary offence and for a crime, or whether he would be only be processed for a crime? "A. It would be only for a crime either for a murder or an attempted murder, and that the decision of the military court, if we're talking about that time, will envelope or consume the same person's military disciplinary responsibility. If you will allow me, I would like to say something else. If the military court were to find that person guilty of a crime, of murder or attempted murder, I allow myself to assume that that person would be dishonourably discharged from the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia as well." Then he says, at page 11688, lines 17 to 20: "I simply cannot envisage a situation where person A, an active duty serviceman, is being tried before a military court for murder, and that a military disciplinary proceedings are conducted before the military disciplinary Tribunal for the same offence." Now, I ask you, Mr. Theunens, in interpreting Article 31 of the Code of Disciplinary Conduct, isn't it correct that when it comes to crime, it was assumed that the offenders disciplinary responsibility would be enveloped by the criminal proceedings, but that in circumstances where the commander felt it was necessary to initiate disciplinary proceedings as well, because there was some interest of the service implicated, he could do that at his discretion? Isn't that the right way to interpret Article 31.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just read out Article 31, and I have given you my understanding of it; that is, that - and I start then with the second part of what you read out - Article 31 deals with the role of the authorised officer, i.e., the commander. It doesn't address what the military courts are doing or what the military disciplinary courts are doing. It simply states that that the military commander has the right to initiate disciplinary proceedings if he thinks that this is in the interest of the service. Obviously, then if the matter is taken over - and now we're talking about time factor - the matter is taken over by the military prosecutor and justice is rendered there, there is no need anymore for a disciplinary procedure. But prior to that, if the commander thinks that it is important for the service, the article allows him to also initiate disciplinary procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Theunens, let me take you to Exhibit P71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you page 69 of P71, Mr. Theunens, which is the Split Military District operational diary. This page was not included in your report because for some reason it was never translated, so I don't know if you have ever seen this page or not. Have you seen the most revised version of P7?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That also explains the numerous entries in the corrigendum to change references of page numbers to entries in the operational diary in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on that a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now after Grahovo, and General Gotovina -- and, again, this was never translated when your report was done. It says, towards the middle of that first entry: "The biggest problem in OG Sjever," which is OG North, "is the lack of discipline. So we ordered to the commanders of the units to pay attention and strictly forbid looting and burning." That was something you had not seen when you wrote area report, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, but I have seen it afterwards. But it is line in what I have seen in the other parts of the diary; as well, it is coherent by orders issued by General Gotovina throughout and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the commander of Operative Group North?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any documents showing an operative role for Brigadier Glasnovic during Operation Storm, but I believe that during Maestral, or the operation afterwards, he again occupies a command position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, are you under the impression that General Glasnovic was the commander of the OG North on the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who is the commander of OG North on the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Ademi is the commander according to the order Kozjak 95, dated 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. But who is the commander of OG North on the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on this entry, it's Glasnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to Exhibit D793, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is General Gotovina's order from the 3rd of August, and he says: "In keeping with the order for attack and with the purpose of having a uniform command and control of the units, I order: Staff Brigadier Rahim Ademi is temporarily appointed commander of OG North. He shall perform the said duty along side his establishment duty." Point 2: "The outgoing commander of the OG North, Colonel Slaven Zdilar, is to resume his duty of acting chief of infantry of Split Military District command." Now, can you tell me -- first, from a military prospective, tell us, when somebody is appointed chief of the infantry in a command, that's not a very high-ranking position, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a command position, but the document says he is to resume his duty. So I understand from that, that he had that duty before. Operational Groups are temporary arrangements, i.e., they do not exist in peacetime. They are set up to carry out particular operations during a particular time-period, which means that the command positions there are also an ad hoc issue. When there is no need anymore for the OG, well, then the other commander resumes, will return to his regular duties. We see that also with the commanders of the OGs that are established in Kozjak 95, these are all officers who, with the exception of Brigadier Ademi, hold a command position within units of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there's a little bit different issue here than the one you just answered, which is that Operative Group North was not, as you say -- you said, "when there is no need for the operative group, then the commander will return to his regular duties." Clearly, on the 3rd of August, there was a need for Operative Group North; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was just giving a theoretical answer to explain how OGs are established or why they are established, and also to point out that the command thing. We do, indeed, see here that General Gotovina replaces the commander of OG North.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have seen and I have already taken you through Mr. Lausic' notes from the meeting of the 2nd of August, so I won't go through that again. First, let me ask you: When you were preparing your report or preparing area addendum, were you aware that Ambassador Galbraith had a meeting with President Tudjman on the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a specific meeting on the 1st of August. I have seen former President Tudjman, or the late-President Tudjman, on the BBC series, "The Death of Yugoslavia," where he spoke about last minute contacts with the US Ambassador Galbraith, and I know from my duties in the UNPF headquarters that, until the last moment, there were close contacts between the Croatian authorities and its main allies in the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you follow Ambassador Galbraith's testimony here in this case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen five minutes of it, but I was working on other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that Ambassador Galbraith spelled out certain conditions to President Tudjman regarding the treatment of civilians and the treatment of UNCRO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This seems to correspond with what President Tudjman stated through "The Death of Yugoslavia," but I'm not familiar of the specifics of what Ambassador Galbraith said to Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I said, you have seen now the notes from the 2nd of August in Mr. Lausic' diary about the meeting with Minister Susak, Chief of Staff Cervenko, and all military commanders about preventing, burning, and looting; treating UNPROFOR well; et cetera. We've gone through the MUP and military police coordination meetings, so I won't repeat those again. With respect to orders passed by General Gotovina, I think -- first, let me call your attention to page 113 of your report, part 2, paragraph small Roman numeral ii. I just wanted to draw your attention to it. This is from what is now marked in evidence as Exhibit D201.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this accurately reflects General Gotovina's attack order to the political affairs branch to react vigorously and in good time, in cases of disorganisation, undermining of the command system, relations, discipline, incidents of panic, prevention of looting and burning; and, also, accurately reflects that there was an order given to pass along how to treat civilians and POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. That's what D201 states. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me go to Exhibit P1126, please, page3, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the order the attachment to the SIS which also, at number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is on page 3 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That order says: "Prevent burning and looting of facilities in the liberated territory, immediately station personnel of the MUP, special MUP units, and VP in large towns to secure the town an important buildings." So do we agree that, prior to Operation Storm, General Gotovina passed orders to both the political affairs branch and the SIS to inform units about their obligations under the Geneva Conventions and to prevent burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we looked at P71, you can tell me if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have P71, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we have already talked about the entry on the evening of the 4th of August, where the assistant commander for political affairs says, at the meeting, essentially, burning and looting must be prevented, Knin must not suffer the same fate as Grahovo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you classify that as a warning by the political affairs officer to General Gotovina and others present. In point of fact, isn't it really a warning to the other commanders? He is not warning General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just assist me and tell me on which page I have mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it, I believe. Is it English page 324?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's one of them. I believe there is -- just one second.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on English page 324, I state: "During the Split Military District Command working meeting on 4th of August in the evening, the assistant commander for political affairs of the Split Military District informs the attendees, including Gotovina, that morale in the Split Military District units is good, adding Knin must not experience the same treatment as Grahovo, and that burning and destruction should be prevented."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I call your attention to page 311, subparagraph H. There you wrote: "The chief of the Split Military District political department ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak in the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The chief of the Split Military District political department warns Colonel-General Ante Gotovina and other members of the Split MD command that Knin should not experience the same treatment as Grahovo, and that burning and destruction should be prevented."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, that is the summary section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He is not warning General Gotovina; right? He is acting, amongst other things, pursuant to an order that General Gotovina gave him the day before or two days before. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. It is not a warning in military sense. It is maybe an unfortunate choice of word in the summary section, but, again, the summary -- for those who want to know more about the summary, they will go into the report; and then on page 3124, you have the exact quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could go in P71 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, am I correct in understanding that your question comprised two matters: First of all, whether it was a warning or not; and, second, whether it was as a result of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not heard an answer to that question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Based on the fact that General Gotovina had issued this order on the 2nd to the political affairs officer, would it be your conclusion that is he acting at the meeting pursuant to what his duties are pursuant to the attack order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I'm looking for the English page that begins at 5 August, which is page 87 in the English. And we're having a more difficult time finding the Croatian, but it could be page 49 in the Croatian. Actually, if we can now go back one or two pages, I need the morning of the 5th of August. It's page 84. The entry is at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you see on the right-hand side, this is now at 9.40 in the morning on the 5th, when HV troops are in the process of entering Knin. It is recorded that General Gotovina orally issued an order that said that he ordered maximum fairness in treatment of civilians and behaviour towards UN. This was passed to all OG and commanders; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you include that in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, but I'm not sure where. But in any event, the diary, as such, is also included. I have included-- if it is the issue of the behaviour towards UN, I have included the order by General Gotovina, as well as the entries in the war diary in relation to the activities of the commander of the Split garrison, or the problems there were between him and UNCRO, including also the order by General Gotovina to have him arrested, and to instruct, again, all his subordinates to apply maximum fairness towards UNCRO personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk a bit about Knin on the 5th of August. You cited the document -- you cited the document by Colonel Zelic where he reports about the "catastrophic" affairs in Knin on the 5th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful if I could have the page number in my report. But if I put words between quotation marks, it means that I quoted from the document; that is, it's not my use of words, but it's the word that is used or the text that comes from the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not challenging that that word comes in the original document. What I'd like to go through right now is what was really taking place in Knin and what exactly did this individual find in Knin that he described as catastrophic. I think you will agree with me that "catastrophic" is a relative term; right? What might be catastrophic for you might not be catastrophic for me, or we may use that word to mean various different things?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would know that a senior offers with the rank of colonel who is the assistant commander for political affairs in the Split Military District knows why he uses the words used in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let see if we can agree on things. Do we agree that there weren't or that there is not reporting in the documents of HV troops murdering civilians in Knin on the 5th or the 6th?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you point me in my report where I refer to that document or could we see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's page 325.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a quote on paragraph 3 on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He says the treatment of property was catastrophic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I see it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, now, when we talk about the treatment of property being catastrophic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, if we could go -- I don't know if Mr. Waespi can help me with the P number on that document by Mr. Zelic. P1133, Mr. Registrar. Thank you. If we can go to the next page, please, and if we go to the middle of -- I'm sorry, the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He reports: "The entry itself of our members and the treatment of civilians was proper and at the required level. However, the behaviour of our members regarding property found was catastrophic. Immediately after entry, the devastation of buildings and uncontrolled collection of war booty began, but military police units had already entered the town and manned the main check-points, preventing further destruction and devastation of property."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we go to - let me see - Exhibit P1134, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Tomasovic's report, I believe -- I am sorry. It's Zeljko Pavic, assistant commander for SIS in OG North, who provides further details on what this catastrophic treatment of property was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to page 5 in the English, please. I seem to have a different page 5. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Morale and discipline. It says: "We were not informed of any cases of disobedience or breaches of the discipline code during combat operations. As members of the 7th and 4th Guards Brigade entered the town of Knin, commanders lost control over some individuals who were taking various ... items and technical equipment from groceries, other shops, and flats. This was seen by foreign journalists who were authorised to say in Knin ..." So the reports that you saw, they don't reference, for example, burning of buildings in Knin on the 5th and the 6th. When they talk about devastation of property, they're talking about breaking and entering, breaking glass on store fronts, et cetera, and taking items from shop, groceries, and flats; right? Do you agree that's what you found on the reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we can compare the two reports we saw in the one by Zelic and this one. I have not seen in these two documents any specific information in relation to the burning of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. Well, that was on the 5th and the 6th, and I call your attention to some documents --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you having worked in UNCRO in Zagreb during this time, you were aware that Mr. Akashi went to Knin on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. I worked in the UNPF headquarters, and UNCRO was a subordinate headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably did. I don't recall exactly when Mr. Akashi went to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could, Mr. Registrar, please put on the screen Exhibit D29, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you two documents, so I'm not going to ask you a question just in interests of some time. This is a memo from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan on 7 August after his trip to Knin, where he advises Mr. Annan, as follows in paragraph 2. He says: "My overall impression of the town of Knin is that it suffered considerable damage from artillery fire which was evident in the street, where I observed many shops with broken windows, cars damaged and off the road, artillery shell holes in the road, et cetera. However, the damage to the town's structures, while noticeable, was less than I anticipated. Large numbers of homes and buildings were left untouched by the fighting." So when we're talking about how Mr. Akashi found Knin on the 7th, he notes the damage. He say there is artillery damage, shells -- holes in the streets, damage to shops, broken windows, cars damaged, but he doesn't note any mass burnings or things of that nature that had taken place in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to Exhibit D272, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a memorandum from Peggy Hicks, who is a human rights officer, reporting to a Mr. Harston, having interviewed displaced persons at Sector South HQ on the 6th of August. You can look through the report, I don't have a problem with that, but I'm more interested in just the end. She qualifies her comments first by saying: "Given the small number of people who have been interviewed so far, and the fact that the experiences of this group of displaced people may be quite different from those encountering different Croatian forces in different areas, this information is far from sufficient to reach each preliminary conclusions as to the extent the human rights violations which may have occurred during the Croatian offensive. These interviews do indicate, however, that at least some Croatian soldiers had been given clear and effective instructions to treat civilians in an appropriate manner." Now, when we talk about this report about catastrophic and the treatment of property, do we -- do you agree that, in your review of the documents, there was no indication in the documents that you reviewed that the HV improperly treated civilians upon its entry in Knin on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I have not seen an HV document indicating that there was improper treatment of civilians in Knin on the 5th. In my report, there are documents included, for example, for Benkovac, which indicate the situation there was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can move to the next point, which is the state of Knin on the 7th --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And forgive me if I'm repeating myself, I'm on medication so I may be a little foggy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It hasn't struck me yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, given Mr. Akashi's report and your review of the documents, that the -- the damage to property that we're talking about basically is damage that had occurred as a result of breaking and entering premises and artillery damage that Mr. Akashi referenced. That is not what Mr. Zelic is talking about, and that's why I'm specifically asking that question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I have nothing to add what Colonel Zelic writes in his report that he qualified the treatment of property in a particular manner; and then, okay, we have another document dealing with the visit of Mr. Akashi. But all we can conclude from these two documents is, indeed, that property has not been treated properly; whereas, according to these documents and also this one from front of us, that the treatment of civilians at least based on the information available on the 6th of August to the UN was appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there is an video of a meeting that General Gotovina held on the 6th of August in the morning, where he is reacting to some of the things that we're talking about now. I believe you've seen the video; correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I'm not sure whether I saw it in its entirety, but I'm familiar with the video and the setting and atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That video is not referenced in your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of its existence when the report was filed. I first saw it when -- yeah. I was following the trial proceedings, and then I saw the video. I tried to find a document because I understood that the video was taken during an official meeting. I would expect that there would also have been a report of the meeting and maybe particular instructions issued -- written traces of particular instructions issued during the meeting, and I have not come across such documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which I found unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about that. Zelic's report which uses the word "catastrophic" is written on the evening of the 6th. General Gotovina - and I'm not going to show the whole video now because we have seen it many times in this case - has the meeting with the commanders including Mr. Zelic on the morning of the 6th. Is it possible that Mr. Zelic's reaction, including the use of the word "catastrophic," is as a direct result of General Gotovina and his reaction on the morning of the 6th? And if you note it on the video, he specifically calls out "Mr. Zelic" in the video. Do you think maybe Mr. Zelic used the word "catastrophic" and reported on these things because General Gotovina himself had publicly in front of his colleagues called him out on failures to take certain measures?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that only Mr. Zelic can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I even can answer that question. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At least in my next question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is: You did an addendum, as well, in your report. I believe when you met with us in January, we had raised the issue of the video with you. When you're reconstructing what happened in Sector South and trying to interpret documents such as the Zelic document, tell us, in terms of methodology, why videos in general weren't part of your report, and then, more specifically, why this particular video wasn't in your report? I should just limited it to videos, audio, whatever the electronic method may be?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that one of the problems with videos is that it is not always easy to link the images one sees to particular event, and, more specifically, to establish the correct timing of these images. For example, the video of the meeting, I'm not sure whether the date is mentioned during the meeting. For me, it is not sufficient that there's a subtitle like "6 August," because anyone can do that. Without going into too many details, in my previous job, we received videos from the various embassies in Brussels of various parties involved in conflict. Most of them dealt with destroyed houses and not very pleasant pictures of war victims. It would happen that two different sides would send us the same images but with a different date and, in their view, a different party who was responsible for these gruesome acts. So, again, to cut it short, videos are difficult because it is not always easy to identify the correct context and, in particular, the correct date. That was one of my problems with the -- the video of the meeting you talk about. And as I mentioned, I looked for documents and I couldn't find a document in relation to that meeting, which I found unusual, because there you see that the highest operational commander in the area gives very clear warnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me note a few things about the video. If you watched it, then would you have noted them yourself. General Gotovina, as well as General Cermak, both reference that at 5.00, senior officials from the Croatian government - they mention the prime minister, et cetera - are coming at 5.00. General Gotovina mentions turning it over to the civilian government at 5.00, and he looks at his watch at one point on the video and says: It 11.30. You should have been doing this since 4.00 this morning." Now, you're an information officer. I'm sure, in your job, you have had to piece information like this together to reconstruct what day we're talking about. But what date do you know the senior highest level officials came to Knin for the first time at 5.00?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned the visit by President Tudjman in my report, but I'm not sure anymore whether it was on the 6th or the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I think the issue is quite clear, that you've seen a video. You say it's difficult to see whether the date is correct. Mr. Misetic is now verifying whether it would have been possible, on the basis of what you have seen, to express even if not a final opinion on whether the date and the time was correct or not. Did you make an effort to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then your answer was evasive, the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was evasive to the extent that you said, "It was very difficult, videos, et cetera. It is unusual." The other way of dealing with it, as an expert, is to see what clues you find in such a video, which would allow you with certainty or probability to see whether the time and the date of this video was correct. Then to pay further attention to the fact that apparently such important matters happened without leaving any paper trace, because that's what you're telling us. Would you please refrain from evasive answers and address the matters that Mr. Misetic puts to you. Mr. Misetic, I am also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there is an technical matter. Did you intend to play the video you had on mind right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was my plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no problem with that, but the transcriber has asked whether it would be allowed to cut and paste, because there is a text put on paper already. Of course, the transcript should reflect literally what is said. Now the technique used by our interpreters, especially if speed goes up - I think that was agreed upon - is that the English transcript which has been distributed among the parties is read by one of the interpreters and that the other interpreter checks whether what is found on the transcript reflects what is said in the original. We have developed this technique because often we can't slow down speakers on video. I wish that we could, but we can't do that. So if we would rely on cutting and pasting, that would require from everyone to see that nothing else is interpreted, spoken, then the text, as we find it on the English transcript, which is put on paper, I would allow, therefore, cutting and pasting. At the same time, if anything happens which results in words spoken not exactly as this appear on the written transcript as it has been distributed, then, of course, we would have to correct that. With this proviso, you can play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Obviously, we have no objection to that; and in line with the last time we played a rather lengthy, we will do the pausing every minute or two minutes to allow the interpreters and the court reporter, if necessary, to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be good to stop any how now and then, because even reading the text, you may easily get behind rather soon. So there is nothing wrong in stopping now and then, but, I think, in this way we make it -- we at least assist in our transcribers and interpreters to do their job as reliable as they always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what I'd like to show you is now -- as I indicated to you before, there was a video-clip which was put into evidence earlier in this case, which was Exhibit D792. That was a clip from a meeting in Knin on the 6th of August. There was a continuation of that meeting which I will call the second part of the meeting which was never shown in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just so you are aware, the Prosecution had a heavily-edited video of that portion of the meeting which they wanted to bar table. We have in the meantime acquired the unedited portion of the video, taken from a different camera. We believe, if you wish I can highlight later, but there are certain important elements that was given to OTP, which was given to them in that fashion, that are deleted from the video that was produced to the Office of the Prosecutor. That's why we wish to play the entire clip, so the Trial Chamber understanding exactly everything that is transpiring on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it, of course, raises the question why redacted versions are provided to the OTP. I don't know whether it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can address that partially, Your Honour, which is that, as I said, there were at least two cameras at that meeting. The -- the video that the Prosecution received was edited from that one camera. I won't go into details now. We have had problems with that provider as well, providing unedited material. We then were able to get in contact with the second camera, and got the unedited portion of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have the raw material now, so to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only issue of ours is to have the entire video, you know, unedited as much as we can, uninterrupted, and, you know, I'm sure we can work to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I mean, to make it perfectly clear, I think did I that, but under no circumstances was I suggesting untoward concerning the Prosecution. I believe they were produced a video that had been heavily edited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let look at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this video is 1D63-0055.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Gotovina: Special units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and we switch there to defense. We shall see further how the situation in the field shall evolve for the other HV units which advance in the direction of Western Bosnia and link up and emerge to the Croatian border. Until then, this is the goal which should be met; and, this way, we put the security of the Zagreb-Knin-Split railroad under control, where the Ministry of Transport as of Monday automatically shall begin with cleaning the tracks from Split towards Knin and from Zagreb towards Knin. The railroad shall become operable. "This task of emerging here, we cannot lose time or fatigue our forces who have been in combat up to now; rather, we have to complete this as soon as possible. On Tuesday, finish this and transfer to defense in this area. The attack forces, i.e. the 81st HV Brigade, the Guards Zdrug, the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade, the 4th Guards Brigade, the 7th Guards Brigade, handover the complete area where we include all the other forces of the 2nd Echelon in defense. The remaining forces are let go into the waiting area for rest, and we await the next order and task by the Supreme Commander. Is this clear? "Commander of the Zadar group? "Unknown Male: It's clear, General. "Gotovina: Commander of the Šibenik group? "Unknown Male: Clear. "Gotovina: Commander of the Sinj group? "Unknown Male: It's clear. I shall withdraw the majority of my ..." "Gotovina: You withdraw exactly the 3rd Battalion of the 126th Regiment (the 3rd Battalion of the 126th Home Guards Regiment) for leave, because it is an offensive regiment, and the remaining forces switch to defense. "Commander of the 4th Guards brigade, clear? "DK: Clear. "Gotovina: Commander of the 7th Guards Brigade, the 81st Guards Brigade, the Zdrug? "Unknown Male: Clear. "Gotovina: The 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade, you pass this on. He is working today. "Unknown Male: Working. "Gotovina: We are following this evening. Report on your exact position by 2000 hours. This especially pertains to the Šibenik and Zadar groups; That is, the Zadar group and the Sibenik group. The Sinj group has completed its task for the most part. So you await only this part of the shift of the 6th Regiment towards the top and the area is closed off. "Unknown Male: We shall complete this today. "Gotovina: That is the operational task which we have. Did the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade prepare a cocktail for the commanders? "Unknown Male: [Indiscernible] "Gotovina: No, no. "IK: Everything is outside, coffee, juice. "Unknown Male: Mr. General. "Gotovina: Yes. "Unknown Male: The 142nd Regiment had -- it completed ... linking up with the HVO at [indiscernible]. There are large areas for mopping-up. "Gotovina: Yes. "Unknown Male: So that we'll have to use them for at least one day. "Gotovina: All the military that I mentioned that is going towards Knin, they have nothing to do in Knin. It is only to encircle Knin. Do you understand? It comes to the peripheral entrance of the town itself. "IC: All roads will be closed off. No one will be permitted to enter without a permit as of tomorrow. "Gotovina: Yes, there won't be access; Therefore, the periphery of the town in encircled by the defense forces. Entry into the town is forbidden, And those defense forces are not all there 100 per cent. The remaining forces are oriented towards the areas which are still -- or which we still consider to be problematic. Mopping-up is to be carried out. Are you clear now on what [indiscernible] this group, the Sibenik group? "Kotlar, is everything all right? "DK: Everything is all right. "Gotovina: You carry on. I sent you Marko Rajcic there, in fact, the Sibenik group, the Military District artillery chief, so that the task in that area is completed as soon as possible. You have Beneta as reinforcement; meaning, you have all the necessary conditions to fulfill this in any case, the equipment, the ammunition, and everything necessary, to fulfill this task as soon as possible. "The remainder, the second thing that needs to be solved in a planned manner is the issue of all this war booty. It must be completely logged. The logistics of the Military District must have full lists, logs of all the war booty, ammunition, and everything else. "Exactly, in order to be able to submit this to the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defense, which will subsequently know what we have at this moment at our disposal in order to be able to plan the upcoming tasks, and so we can begin the reassignment of materiel for those units which shall remain active in order to equip themselves well and in order for us to be prepared for the execution of the following tasks. "Is this understood commanders? "Therefore, the discipline of conducting this task depends on you; meaning, you are the ones who are supposed to initiate this issue with your logistics assistant and with the logistics of the military district in order to solve this problem. "Finally, yesterday, following the entrance of the units, primarily into Knin, of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigades, which have worked on this task all this time from the beginning of October by breaking through the most difficult areas, an unforgiving terrain, harsh climate, and all the other problems we've had, including, as you know, the possibilities of our state to support us logistically. They certainly accomplished their task and, indeed, solved this problem of this key political and military epicenter, which certainly caused all the rest that was standing like a house of cards to come crushing down. "Now, all you other commanders have also accomplished your tasks. It's important that all these larger places like Benkovac, Obrovac, Kistanje, Djevrske, Drnis, that's all solved. So, we're continuing up, further on. Yesterday, at 1330 hours, the minister of defense called, and after that the Supreme Commander, who congratulated all the units who took part in the offensive operation and all the commanders who led these units in the offensive operation. "Now that we've more or less accomplished somewhere around 70 per cent of our task, we still have this target, to come out to this target, which is the value of the operation, the ultimate value of the operation, putting traffic into operation; that is to say, Zagreb-Knin-Split. We will resolve this by Tuesday certainly. At the moment, we're writing a report to the Supreme Command: Task accomplished 100 per cent at the Split Military District with the forces, the Croatian forces of the Croatian Defense Council. "Where are the commanders of the 1st, 2nd , 3rd Guards Brigades? "Unknown Male: Mr. General, they are in the field. "Gotovina: I said they were to be at the meeting this morning, Glasnovic. The Commanders of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd, the commander of the 4th command post the Group North were supposed to be here at the meeting. "We are now faced with the next problem we have; that is, all those structure, the others, the remaining structures, the logistics, political activity, security, military police, and everybody else that follows an army in an offensive, which automatically protects the army during the offensive, that step ahead and step behind. Automatically, these structures assume everything that remains to be solved, in order for everything to be in order, militarily in total order, completely solved. The guarantee for military culture and for the military reputation of and army is its political activity, security service, military police. "You are the most responsible people here for all this mess that we have here. This is why we have five hours until then, five hours to get the town itself in order, and that it be equipped with everything necessary to await the Croatian leadership. Do you understand? "Any questions? Perkovic. "Unknown Male: General, are we still supposed to relocate the command post here, and I'm interested in the time, so that I could put up the PZO because we have to [indiscernible] well. "Gotovina: That will be done by the commander of the military -- military Command center, the logistics, and the chief operations officer. They shall decide when they are technically prepared to transfer the command and when the conditions are met to run the command from the FCP in Knin. You will be informed when in due time. "Go ahead, Krsticevic. "DK: I would also ask, so considering I already -- you already spoke of this, that urgently also I mean from here - considering my command, I mean - to the 'Southern Barracks,' in order to coordinate, by wire or Motorola, with a part of the Zadar Operations Group, Mr. Fuzul and I, meaning with a part of those that are going from Djevrske and Kistanje, so that there wouldn't be any shooting among, to avoid -- "Gotovina: That's very important. The communications chiefs of all units should contact each other, elaborate maps, positions. "Unknown Male: So that we are able to reach each other, in order to be able -- "MF: Mr. General, already last night, I organized with the Prefect, where I expect that this afternoon we shall have a connected Benkovac-Zadar switchboard, and that we will be able to transfer the FCP and everything to Benkovac. I expect that this will be solved during the afternoon. "Gotovina: Then Benkovac, Djevrske, Kistanje, Knin to be coordinated. "Unknown Male: They shall be coordinated, the HPT, the Directorate of the Zadar Center, promised me he'd make efforts to get this functioning this afternoon. "Gotovina: Okay. "Unknown Male: This way we will surely [indiscernible] for Knin.
